title: Data Loss Prevention
summary: Data Loss Prevention, usually shortened to DLP, is the combination of classification and enforcement that watches how sensitive data moves and stops the movements policy forbids. The mechanism runs in layers: data is discovered and labelled by pattern, fingerprint or document matching, then inspected in motion at endpoints, network egress and cloud services, where a policy engine decides to log, warn, quarantine, encrypt or block. Effective programmes start with data discovery and a small number of high confidence rules, because noisy rules that block ordinary work get disabled by the people they annoy. In real environments DLP shows up in email gateways, secure web gateways, endpoint agents, cloud access security brokers and cloud storage sharing controls. Evidence includes incident records with the rule that matched, the file or data type, the destination, the user and the action taken, plus the tuning history that shows false positives being reduced.

beginner.definition: Data loss prevention is a set of tools and rules that watch sensitive information. It looks at where that information is and where it is going. If a transfer breaks your rules, the tool can warn the user, record the event, or stop it. It protects both personal data and company secrets.
beginner.whyItMatters: Sensitive data leaves an organisation in many ways, and most of them are accidental. A spreadsheet emailed to the wrong person, a file uploaded to a personal cloud drive, or a support ticket with customer details inside. Deliberate theft follows the same paths, which makes these controls useful for both. Regulations also expect you to know where personal data lives and who can send it out. Without this visibility you find out about a leak from a stranger.
howItWorks: Find and label the sensitive data you hold, such as personal details, health records and design documents.
Write clear rules that say which data may go to which places and under what conditions.
Place sensors where data moves, on endpoints, email, web traffic and cloud storage.
Inspect the traffic and compare each item against your rules before it leaves.
Choose an action, such as logging, warning the user, encrypting the file or blocking the transfer.
Review the alerts, fix the noisy rules and repeat, because tuning decides whether this works.
beginner.example: Picture a post office where a clerk knows which documents are private. Before sealing an envelope, the clerk checks the address and the contents against a list. Mostly the clerk stamps and sends as normal. For one sensitive page going to a private address, the clerk stops and asks a supervisor. The list is short, clear and reviewed often, so queues keep moving.
takeaways: Know and label your sensitive data first, because a rule cannot protect data you have not found.
Start with a few high confidence rules, since noisy blocking gets switched off by frustrated staff.
Cover endpoints, email, web and cloud, because data leaves through more than one door.

objectives: Explain how classification, inspection and policy enforcement combine in a DLP programme.
Describe where DLP sensors sit across endpoint, network and cloud environments.
Identify the data types a programme should protect and how they are discovered.
Recognise why false positives lead to control failure and how tuning reduces them.
List the evidence a DLP incident record should contain for investigation.
